Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows broad cover of low non-woody vegetation with sparse to absent tree canopy, unlike Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears as irregular natural-looking vegetation patches rather than the neat rectangular parcels of Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks visible crop rows or plow-line striping that often marks Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land does not show the ordered orchard or vineyard grid typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has diffuse shifting boundaries in the vegetation instead of sharply defined field edges.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land presents a soft fine texture from low plants without the dark clustered crowns seen in Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land forms open expanses with very few shadows from tall vegetation or structures.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often mixes green and tan tones in a mottled natural pattern rather than a uniform planted pattern.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows continuous grassy cover interrupted only by occasional bare patches, not by systematic planting structure.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears less subdivided than Pasture Land, with few visible paddock lines or internal fence traces.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land usually lacks the small circular or worn focal spots that can make Pasture Land look more managed.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has a loose uneven patchwork of low vegetation rather than the repeated spacing of Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no regular alternation of bands or strips across fields, helping separate it from Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is dominated by open herb cover with only occasional isolated shrubs or small trees, not continuous woodland.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often extends across terrain as a broad natural color field without parcel-by-parcel agricultural geometry.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows irregular edges that blend gradually into nearby cover instead of the clean borders common in managed fields.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the dense dark canopy mass and coarse crown texture that define Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears visually less managed than Pasture Land because internal divisions and access tracks are sparse or absent.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows low, even vegetation height from above, without row shadows, tree lines, or orchard blocks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has scattered subtle tonal variation across open ground rather than the repeated organized planting patterns of crop land.
Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land shows large arable parcels with straight edges and regular geometric shapes.
Annual Crop Land appears as a patchwork of rectangular or square fields rather than a continuous grassy cover.
Annual Crop Land displays clear parcel boundaries that separate neighboring fields into distinct units.
Annual Crop Land often includes adjacent fields in different seasonal states, from bare soil to low green cover.
Annual Crop Land has visible exposed soil across many parcels, unlike Pasture Land which looks more continuously vegetated.
Annual Crop Land shows orderly field geometry rather than the diffuse irregular texture of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land contains broad cultivated plots whose layout is clearly human-made and aligned in repeated directions.
Annual Crop Land has smooth to lightly textured field interiors without the dense repetitive row pattern typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land lacks the tightly spaced tree or vine rows that give Permanent Crop Land a striped texture.
Annual Crop Land shows mixed tones between neighboring parcels because different fields are bare, sprouting, or recently harvested.
Annual Crop Land is crossed by straight farm tracks or roads that follow field edges and reinforce a grid-like layout.
Annual Crop Land appears dominated by cultivated parcels, with buildings present only as small scattered elements.
Annual Crop Land does not show dense roof clusters or street blocks like Residential Buildings.
Annual Crop Land has low vertical structure, so fields appear open with little shadow from tall objects.
Annual Crop Land often forms expansive mosaics of similarly sized fields rather than irregular natural patches.
Annual Crop Land shows stronger contrast between parcels than Pasture Land, where surfaces are usually more uniform.
Annual Crop Land presents sharper straight borders than Herbaceous Vegetation Land, which lacks a managed field pattern.
Annual Crop Land usually has only a few isolated farm compounds separated by wide cultivated areas.
Annual Crop Land displays repeated field divisions over a broad area, making the scene read as cropland rather than settlement.
Annual Crop Land combines regular parcel geometry with low crop cover, distinguishing it from Permanent Crop Land, Pasture Land, and Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings show a few very large rectangular roofs instead of the many small varied roofs seen in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings are commonly surrounded by broad paved service yards that are much larger than the driveways or gardens around Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings often include loading bays or dock lines along one side of a large building.
Industrial Buildings frequently have trailer parking areas with long rows of parked rectangular units beside warehouses.
Industrial Buildings may contain container stacks or grouped storage blocks in open paved yards.
Industrial Buildings are arranged as large boxy structures separated by truck courts rather than by a dense grid of small local streets.
Industrial Buildings usually have internal roads with wide turning radii designed for heavy vehicles, unlike the narrow street pattern of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings often form ordered compounds with a few large buildings and large open hardstand areas.
Industrial Buildings typically appear as clusters of warehouses with flat bright or gray roofs covering most of each parcel.
Industrial Buildings can show open rectangular storage yards directly attached to the main buildings.
Industrial Buildings often have parking lots sized for trucks or large service vehicles rather than only small car parking.
Industrial Buildings usually occupy large blocks with few intersections, unlike Residential Buildings with many short street segments.
Industrial Buildings often sit on continuous paved parcels, unlike Annual Crop Land or Permanent Crop Land which show planted soil or orchard row textures.
Industrial Buildings lack the repeated field rows and vegetation patterns that identify Annual Crop Land and Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings frequently include long narrow service corridors or rail spurs crossing the site.
Industrial Buildings commonly have buildings aligned in parallel rows with consistent spacing across the complex.
Industrial Buildings often display simple box-shaped footprints with attached apron-like paved areas on multiple sides.
Industrial Buildings usually present fewer but much bigger structures than Residential Buildings, making roof size the dominant visual cue.
Industrial Buildings are set back from public roads behind large paved forecourts instead of fronting directly onto a Highway or Road as a linear transport feature.
Industrial Buildings often appear as enclosed complexes bounded by perimeter roads or fence-like edges around the whole site.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land appears as enclosed grassy parcels bounded by thin hedgerows, fence lines, or narrow tree belts.
Pasture Land shows a fine, even grass texture that is smoother and more homogeneous than rougher Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land lacks the strong parallel crop rows or furrow bands that mark Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land lacks the regular orchard or vineyard grid patterns typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land is mostly open with sparse, discontinuous tree cover rather than the dense canopy of Forest.
Pasture Land often forms a patchwork of adjoining grazing fields separated by visible parcel boundaries.
Pasture Land shows irregular or softly curving field edges instead of rigid rectangular cultivation blocks.
Pasture Land contains grassy parcels with subtle tonal differences between adjacent fields but no row structure.
Pasture Land is crossed by faint livestock tracks or narrow farm lanes within open grass fields.
Pasture Land presents clearly bounded parcels, unlike broad unmanaged grass expanses with weak internal divisions.
Pasture Land includes hedge-defined plots that are more visibly parcelized than Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land shows occasional isolated farm buildings surrounded by much larger grassy enclosures.
Pasture Land has very little exposed soil except for small worn patches near tracks or parcel corners.
Pasture Land displays narrow linear boundaries that divide fields without the dense branching canopy texture of Forest.
Pasture Land often follows drainage lines with thin vegetated edges while remaining predominantly open grass.
Pasture Land appears as contiguous managed grass surfaces broken by fences or hedges rather than by cultivation lines.
Pasture Land shows broad parcels with uniform fine texture and no repeating plantation spacing.
Pasture Land includes scattered small tree clumps mainly along edges, not continuous wooded cover across the parcel.
Pasture Land is organized by enclosed grazing fields that are more regular and bounded than natural Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land shows open green fields divided into paddock-like units without the lineated texture of cropland.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings show many small to medium rooftops packed along a connected grid of neighborhood streets.
Residential Buildings contain numerous compact building footprints rather than a few very large rectangular roofs.
Residential Buildings often appear as rows of homes aligned along short straight or gently curving local streets.
Residential Buildings have a fine-grained texture created by many small structures, unlike the coarse texture of industrial compounds.
Residential Buildings commonly display cul-de-sacs and short branching streets feeding into larger roads.
Residential Buildings feature irregular setbacks between homes and streets instead of uniform warehouse spacing.
Residential Buildings show short driveways and tiny parking pads beside individual buildings rather than expansive paved lots.
Residential Buildings form compact blocks divided by local streets, not long linear transport corridors like highways.
Residential Buildings include small yard-sized green patches between buildings rather than broad continuous field parcels.
Residential Buildings show scattered trees and lawns mixed with houses, not long parallel planting rows like permanent crops.
Residential Buildings break open space into many house lots and blocks instead of homogeneous agricultural fields.
Residential Buildings tend to have moderate to high building density with only narrow gaps between neighboring structures.
Residential Buildings often repeat similarly sized roofs across a neighborhood, creating a uniform small-scale pattern.
Residential Buildings can form suburban layouts with detached homes spread evenly across winding residential roads.
Residential Buildings frequently show intersecting local streets that divide the area into short residential blocks.
Residential Buildings may include apartment blocks that appear as repeated mid-sized rectangles among smaller homes.
Residential Buildings usually lack loading yards, storage pads, and large service courts beside buildings.
Residential Buildings often follow a neighborhood street hierarchy of local roads and collectors rather than a single dominant roadway.
Residential Buildings commonly present fragmented vegetation as backyard patches and street trees rather than planted crop strips.
Residential Buildings generally lack large single-use open parcels, appearing instead as a continuous mosaic of houses, streets, and small lots.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land shows orchard parcels with evenly spaced tree crowns forming a dotted grid.
Permanent Crop Land displays vineyard-like rows running in parallel with consistent spacing inside each field.
Permanent Crop Land has visible inter-row soil between planted lines, unlike the smoother cover of pasture land.
Permanent Crop Land contains strong internal planting texture within parcels, unlike many annual crop fields that look more uniform by field.
Permanent Crop Land appears as small to medium cultivated blocks filled with repeated woody planting patterns.
Permanent Crop Land shows row direction clearly across each parcel, with lines continuing in an organized layout.
Permanent Crop Land features repeated dots or short linear crowns that indicate planted trees rather than open herbaceous cover.
Permanent Crop Land has a textured canopy made of spaced plants, not the dense continuous canopy typical of forest.
Permanent Crop Land presents neat geometric parcels whose interiors are patterned by regular planting spacing.
Permanent Crop Land shows alternating dark vegetation rows and lighter gaps that create a striped appearance.
Permanent Crop Land contains orchard-like fields where individual crowns can be distinguished as separate points.
Permanent Crop Land displays compact parcels with finer and more intensive internal patterning than adjacent annual crop land.
Permanent Crop Land shows planted lines that remain evenly separated across the whole parcel.
Permanent Crop Land appears as organized agricultural land where each field has a repeated within-field grid or row texture.
Permanent Crop Land features woody vegetation arranged in plantations, unlike the softer continuous texture of herbaceous vegetation land.
Permanent Crop Land shows regular crown spacing that is more deliberate and geometric than the irregular structure of forest.
Permanent Crop Land contains parcels where the vegetation pattern is visible inside field boundaries rather than appearing as a smooth solid tone.
Permanent Crop Land displays orchards or vine blocks with consistent row orientation, even when parcel edges curve slightly.
Permanent Crop Land has a repeated plantation texture across contiguous fields, with each parcel showing similar spacing cues.
Permanent Crop Land shows more structured and repetitive planting geometry than pasture land, which lacks clear internal rows or crown grids.
River: River appears as a narrow elongated inland watercourse rather than a broad compact water body like a sea or lake.
River forms a continuous channel that can be traced across the scene from one side to another.
River follows a sinuous winding path instead of the straight engineered line typical of many roads or canals.
River shows broad meanders with smooth outer bends and tighter inner curves visible from above.
River often has irregularly changing width along its course rather than a uniform linear width.
River displays Y-shaped tributary junctions where smaller water channels merge into the main channel.
River is part of a branching dendritic drainage pattern, unlike isolated lakes or single roads.
River contains water-toned surfaces in blue, green, or brown, unlike dry road surfaces or vegetation belts.
River may appear muddy or sediment-laden, giving the channel a brownish or blue-green color.
River can include pale curved point bars on the inner sides of meander bends.
River may show cut-bank contrast on outer bends where the channel edge is sharper and darker.
River sometimes forms oxbow-shaped loops or crescent remnants beside the active channel.
River can split into braided side channels separated by light sand or gravel bars.
River often includes exposed mid-channel sandbars as light patches within the watercourse.
River cuts across fields or forest as a natural curving corridor rather than following a grid or straight route.
River keeps clear upstream-to-downstream continuity through linked channel segments instead of ending as a compact basin.
River may widen locally into pooled reaches before narrowing again farther along the same channel.
River has natural irregular banks that do not maintain the parallel edges typical of highways or canals.
River is usually much longer than it is wide, distinguishing it from rounder inland lakes.
River may traverse herbaceous land or forest as a single connected water line with joined feeder streams.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake covers a broad contiguous water area that is much wider and more open than a narrow river channel.
Sea or Lake shows an interior surface that is largely uninterrupted by tree canopy, grass texture, or field patterns.
Sea or Lake usually has curved shorelines with bays, coves, or rounded margins rather than the thin linear form of a river.
Sea or Lake often forms a large open basin or broad lobe instead of a long branching channel.
Sea or Lake may appear as an enclosed inland water body surrounded on most sides by land, indicating a lake.
Sea or Lake may border an open coast with headlands, beaches, or wave-shaped shoreline, indicating a sea.
Sea or Lake can include harbors, piers, or breakwaters set along a coastal edge.
Sea or Lake often has pale shallow-water bands tracing the shoreline around the darker interior water.
Sea or Lake may contain peninsulas that project into a wide water body and create large coves.
Sea or Lake can show islands as isolated land masses fully surrounded by expansive water.
Sea or Lake has a smooth continuous surface across the center, unlike the textured crowns of forest.
Sea or Lake lacks the fine mottled cover of herbaceous vegetation and instead appears as a uniform open area.
Sea or Lake lacks the fenced or parcel-like texture often visible in pasture land near its shores.
Sea or Lake typically spans a width far greater than roads, canals, or other narrow transport corridors.
Sea or Lake often follows a shoreline with broad arcs and recesses rather than the repeated bends of a river.
Sea or Lake may narrow at outlets or inlets, but the main body remains substantially wider than the connecting channel.
Sea or Lake commonly has shore-to-shore distances large enough that opposite banks are widely separated across open water.
Sea or Lake may show marshy fringes only at the edge, while the central area remains open water.
Sea or Lake often contrasts strongly with adjacent forest, herbaceous land, or pasture because the water body has almost no internal texture.
Sea or Lake presents a dominant open-water mass with broad geometry rather than multiple thin strips or branching threads.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road appears as a long engineered corridor with a uniform width rather than the irregular widening and narrowing of a river.
Highway or Road shows a smooth gray, dark, or pale paved surface instead of the textured water surface of a sea, lake, or river.
Highway or Road often contains two or more parallel lanes that form a broad linear strip.
Highway or Road has sharp, crisp edges that look straighter and more engineered than natural shorelines or riverbanks.
Highway or Road may include a narrow central median separating opposite directions of travel.
Highway or Road can show faint dashed or solid lane markings running along the pavement.
Highway or Road may contain tiny bright vehicle dots aligned along the corridor.
Highway or Road often forms intersections where one paved line meets another at clear angles.
Highway or Road can include curved ramps or loop shapes that create highway interchanges.
Highway or Road may cross another route on an overpass, visible as one linear strip passing above another.
Highway or Road usually reads as a single elongated feature rather than a cluster of many roofed structures.
Highway or Road lacks the large rectangular roof blocks that dominate industrial building areas.
Highway or Road is not dominated by dense small building footprints as in residential neighborhoods.
Highway or Road often appears wider than minor local streets, with a substantial multi-lane corridor.
Highway or Road may have parallel service roads running beside the main paved strip.
Highway or Road can cut across land in a continuous straight or gently curving segment without the branching roof patterns of built complexes.
Highway or Road sometimes appears as an elevated embankment casting a thin linear shadow.
Highway or Road can span dark water as a narrow straight bridge segment with the same width as the approaching pavement.
Highway or Road is typically bordered by narrow shoulders or verges rather than broad water edges or building masses.
Highway or Road stands out as a continuous transportation corridor, not a dense urban street fabric filling whole city blocks.
Forest: Forest shows a dense closed canopy with very few open patches visible from above.
Forest appears as a contiguous dark green to deep olive mass rather than a bright open cover.
Forest has a coarse crown-textured surface created by tightly packed tree tops.
Forest displays mottled shadows and uneven texture instead of the smooth look of herbaceous or pasture land.
Forest lacks the regular planting rows and repeated spacing seen in permanent crop land.
Forest lacks the evenly spaced tree dots or strip patterns typical of orchards and plantations.
Forest lacks the field-by-field parcel mosaic common in annual crop land.
Forest lacks long straight plot boundaries and geometric field divisions visible in cropland.
Forest shows little exposed bare soil compared with annual crop land.
Forest forms large unbroken wooded blocks rather than many small adjacent fields.
Forest has irregular natural edges instead of the straight boundaries of managed agricultural land.
Forest often contains only narrow winding clearings or tracks crossing the canopy.
Forest shows curved internal gaps and access lines rather than straight farm lanes or plot edges.
Forest maintains dark textured cover across slopes and hollows without switching into separate field parcels.
Forest can include small hidden streams or ponds embedded within the tree cover.
Forest presents rounded crown clusters that merge together instead of isolated plants in rows.
Forest appears darker and more textured than surrounding herbaceous vegetation land.
Forest appears darker and less uniform than nearby pasture land.
Forest keeps vegetation as the dominant surface with almost no reflective roofs or paved grid.
Forest shows continuous tree cover across the area rather than alternating cropped strips or seasonal bare patches.
